extracted.intended_audience: young aspiring authors and literary professionals (youthful literati)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and moral counsel for young writers about whether and how to pursue literature: recommends combining writing with a regular profession, careful self-examination of motives, delay before committing to authorship, and standards for journalistic and political writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never pursue literature as a trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Never pursue literature as a trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author’s central charge: do not make authorship a profession dependent on immediate sale or patronage. Treat literary labour as something pursued from tranquil choice rather than necessity; otherwise the stimulant of motive (money/reputation) becomes a narcotic, stunting true genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a regular employment or profession
rubrics_metrics.description: Have some regular employment, which does not depend on the will of the moment, and which can be carried on so far mechanically that an average quantum only of health, spirits, and intellectual exertion are requisite to its faithful discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: manufactory, counting-house, law-court, medical practice, the Church. Benefits: three hours of leisure produce more genial literature than weeks of compulsion; provides financial security, domestic happiness, better public sympathy, and a quicker tact for what general readers admire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide talents and genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Devote your talents to the acquirement of competence in some known trade or profession, and your genius to objects of tranquil and unbiassed choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel to allocate practical abilities toward competence/profession while reserving creative/genial powers for free literary choice; let literature be an augmentation to your life, not its entire coat-of-arms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not write primarily for money or immediate reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Money, and immediate reputation form only an arbitrary and accidental end of literary labour; the necessity of acquiring them will in all works of genius convert the stimulant into a narcotic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning that economic motives or craving for notoriety will reverse their intended stimulatory effect and harm genuine creative output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct strict self-examination of motives and scruples
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertain with strict self-examination whether indolence, restlessness, or a vanity impatient for immediate gratification have not tampered with the judgment and assumed the vizard of humility for the purposes of self-delusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalogue scruples, reduce them to distinct intelligible form, ensure you have read fundamental works on the subject, and, if possible, consult an elder contemporary who had similar scruples and can testify from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay authorship until maturity when in doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: Time spent in such delay is time won: manhood in the meantime is advancing, and with it increase of knowledge, strength of judgment, and above all, temperance of feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postponing a rash commitment to authorship gives intellectual and moral growth that prevents later regret; delay safeguards against decisions made from vanity or impatience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider a profession (notably the Church) compatible with literary pursuits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church presents to every man of learning and genius a profession, in which he may cherish a rational hope of being able to unite the widest schemes of literary utility with the strictest performance of professional duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: parish life transplants a germ of civilization, offers unobtrusive continuous patronage, social standing, access to families across classes, decorum favourable to genius, and models for emulation; other honourable professions similarly support literary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write mainly in leisure rather than under compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: Three hours of leisure, unannoyed by any alien anxiety, and looked forward to with delight as a change and recreation, will suffice to realize in literature a larger product of what is truly genial, than weeks of compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical schedule advice: part-time, voluntary writing preserves quality and creativity; avoids the perverse effects of financial necessity driving content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid publishing every passing thought; resist becoming a 'servant of the press'
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A Mensch, der nur liest um zu drucken... und wer jeden Gedanken, der ihm aufstösst, durch Feder und Presse versendet, hat sie in kurzer Zeit alle versandt, und wird bald ein blosser Diener der Druckerey.’ (Herder: avoid authorship; if used too early it makes the head waste and the heart empty.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make immediate publication the habit; reading merely to publish degrades reading quality and makes the writer a mere mechanic of the printing press. Preserve selection and maturity before dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial consistency: conduct a paper on fixed, announced principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should thenceforwards be conducted on certain fixed and announced principles, and I should neither be obliged nor requested to deviate from them in favour of any party or any event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As editor, publicly state guiding principles and refuse opportunistic deviations for party advantage or transient events; consistency builds trust and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and practice honest impartiality in journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: By impartiality I mean an honest and enlightened adherence to a code of intelligible principles previously announced, and faithfully referred to in support of every judgment on men and events; not indiscriminate abuse, not the indulgence of an editor’s own malignant passions, and still less... a determination to make money by flattering the envy and cupidity... of the half-witted vulgar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impartiality requires principled judgments, avoidance of personal malice, and refusal to pander to base popular appetites for profit; such practice can secure success without ministerial patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place public questions and events in a moral point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing the questions and events of the day in a moral point of view; in giving a dignity to particular measures by tracing their policy or impolicy to permanent principles, and an interest to principles by the application of them to individual measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply moral and principled analysis to contemporary events to give them lasting interest and to make policy debates intelligible and dignified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical comparison and primary sources in political writing
rubrics_metrics.description: On every great occurrence I endeavoured to discover in past history the event, that most nearly resembled it. I procured, wherever it was possible, the contemporary historians, memorialists, and pamphleteers. Then fairly subtracting the points of difference from those of likeness... I conjectured that the result would be the same or different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method for political essays: identify historical analogues, gather original/contemporary accounts, carefully weigh likenesses and differences, and use philosophical tact to judge probable outcomes; examples include comparisons of Napoleon with the Caesars and the United Provinces with Philip II.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure a scholar’s usefulness by intellectual influence, not publication count
rubrics_metrics.description: Would that the criterion of a scholar’s utility were the number and moral value of the truths, which he has been the means of throwing into the general circulation; or the number and value of the minds, whom by his conversation or letters, he has excited into activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value conversational influence, lectures, and the stimulation of other minds equally or more than the mere tally of published volumes when judging a scholar’s contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive refinement, obscurity, and the love of paradox
rubrics_metrics.description: The prose writings have been charged with a disproportionate demand on the attention; with an excess of refinement in the mode of arriving at truths; with the length and laborious construction of my periods; in short with obscurity and the love of paradox.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit corrective: be mindful that over-refinement, needless convolution, and deliberate paradox risk alienating readers; strive for clarity and avoid gratuitous obscurity while not sacrificing depth.
